# Offline Greenhouse Sprayer Build Guide
**Focus: how to build a low-cost sprayer with a fan combination**

## 1) Main goal

You want a sprayer that:

1. makes insecticide into small droplets
2. uses airflow from a fan to move those droplets through the crop leaves
3. reduces the amount of chemical that falls to the ground

That means your best low-cost direction is an **air-assisted mist sprayer**.

This is different from:
- a normal garden sprayer
- a backpack sprayer with no airflow help
- a full fogger that fills the whole room

The best simple target is:

> **fine mist + controlled airflow + short spraying distance**

---

## 2) Best low-cost idea in one sentence

If you are on a budget, the best design is:

> **12V sprayer + filter + pressure gauge + hollow-cone nozzle + 12V blower fan**

That gives you the best balance of:
- cost
- simplicity
- control
- repairability
- easy testing

---

## 3) Ideal particle size

### Short answer

The best practical starting droplet size for your greenhouse idea is:

**50–100 microns**

If you want a simpler target:

**70–100 microns**

### Why this range is best

If droplets are **too big**:
- they fall too fast
- they wet the leaves too much
- they drip off
- more chemical reaches the floor

If droplets are **too small**:
- they float too long
- they spread too far
- they are easier to breathe
- they can evaporate faster
- they become harder to control

### Easy guide

| Droplet size | Meaning | My recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| under 30 μm | fog / aerosol | avoid for cheap DIY insecticide system |
| 30–50 μm | very fine fog | risky and harder to control |
| **50–100 μm** | **mist** | **best starting range** |
| 100–150 μm | fine spray | workable if floor loss stays low |
| over 200 μm | coarse spray | usually too heavy for your purpose |

### Final recommendation

Start around:

> **70–100 μm if possible**

But if you cannot measure exact size, just use:
- a proper hollow-cone nozzle
- suitable pressure
- water-only testing first
- fan tuning

---

## 4) How the system works

The sprayer side makes droplets.

The fan side carries those droplets into the crop.

### Simple flow

```text
Tank
  ↓
Filter
  ↓
Pump
  ↓
Gauge
  ↓
Nozzle
  ↓
Mist
  ↓
Fan air
  ↓
Leaves
```

### Important idea

The fan must catch the droplets **right after** they leave the nozzle.

If the fan is too far away from the nozzle, the spray becomes harder to control.

---

## 5) Best low-cost nozzle type

Use a:

**ceramic hollow-cone agricultural nozzle**

### Why hollow-cone

It is good for:
- finer droplets
- leaf coverage
- insecticide/fungicide style spraying
- better coverage than coarse spray

### Why ceramic

It is usually:
- longer-lasting
- more wear resistant
- better for repeated use

### Do not start with

- thermal fogger parts
- ultrasonic humidifier parts
- tiny perfume misters
- random untested micro-nozzles
- homemade pinhole nozzles

---

## 6) Best fan type

Use a:

**12V inline blower or small centrifugal blower**

### Why a blower is better than a simple open fan

Because the air is more directed.

You want the air to push the mist into the crop, not just move air everywhere.

### Good starting airflow

For a small prototype:
- around **100–200 CFM** is a useful starting range

### Avoid first

- huge greenhouse circulation fans as the main spray fan
- a leaf blower
- a shop blower
- fan motors sitting directly inside wet chemical spray

---

## 7) Best nozzle + fan arrangement

This is the most important mechanical part of the design.

### Good basic concept

```text
[blower] >>>>>>>>

             • • • • fine mist
                nozzle
                  |
                  hose
```

The blower pushes air forward.

The nozzle sprays into that moving air stream.

### Better two-sided aisle setup

```text
Left crop row                    Right crop row
CROP CROP CROP                  CROP CROP CROP

 <<< air + mist                 mist + air >>>

 [fan]-[nozzle]                 [nozzle]-[fan]
        \                         //
         \                       //
          [cart / frame in aisle]
```

### Good starting placement

- nozzle close to blower outlet
- nozzle aimed slightly inward into crop
- fan angled so it catches the mist quickly
- crop distance about 20–40 cm from nozzle to near leaf edge
- leaves should move a little, not violently

---

## 8) Best layout for your greenhouse

If you want a real usable greenhouse tool, I would build:

### Option A — One-sided test unit
Good for first experiments.

Parts:
- one nozzle
- one blower
- one pump
- one tank

Goal:
- check if fan-assisted mist reduces floor loss

### Option B — Two-sided aisle unit
Best practical target.

Parts:
- 2 nozzles minimum
- 2 blowers
- one tank
- one pump
- one cart
- left and right spray supports

Goal:
- spray both crop sides in one pass down the aisle

### Option C — Better working version
After testing:
- 2 to 4 nozzles
- 2 blowers
- two height levels
- adjustable nozzle mounts
- adjustable fan speed
- return line for tank mixing if needed

Goal:
- more even upper + lower canopy coverage

---

## 9) Strong recommendation on number of nozzles

One nozzle works for testing.

But for real plant coverage, **two nozzles per side** is often much better than one.

### Why

Because one nozzle usually covers only one height well.

Two nozzles let you target:
- upper-middle leaves
- middle-lower leaves

### Good two-nozzle-per-side concept

```text
crop side

   upper nozzle  ---> upper-middle canopy
   lower nozzle  ---> lower-middle canopy
```

Angle both slightly inward.

Do not point both straight flat.

## 10) Basic BOM (bill of materials)

### Hydraulic parts

| Part | Purpose | Low-cost suggestion | Rough cost |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Tank | holds liquid | 10–15 gallon tank | $30–$70 |
| Pump | pressurizes liquid | 12V diaphragm pump, 40–70 PSI | $40–$95 |
| Fill screen | stops large dirt | basic screen | $5–$15 |
| Main line filter | protects nozzles | 50-mesh filter | $18–$30 |
| Pressure gauge | pressure reading | 0–60 or 0–100 PSI | $8–$20 |
| Ball valve | on/off | chemical-safe valve | $5–$15 |
| Manifold / tee | split to nozzles | tee or small manifold | $8–$20 |
| Hose | liquid line | chemical-resistant hose | $10–$25 |

### Nozzle parts

| Part | Purpose | Rough cost |
|---|---|---:|
| Ceramic hollow-cone nozzle | fine spray | $6–$13 each |
| Nozzle body / cap | holds nozzle | $3–$10 each |
| Tip strainer | small filter before nozzle | $1–$5 each |
| Spare nozzle | replacement | $6–$13 each |

### Fan/electrical parts

| Part | Purpose | Rough cost |
|---|---|---:|
| 12V blower | move mist into crop | $34–$60 each |
| Fuse | electrical safety | $5–$10 |
| Switch | power control | $5–$12 |
| Wire/connectors | connection | $10–$25 |
| PWM controller (optional) | speed control for fan | $8–$20 |

### Frame/mechanical parts

| Part | Purpose | Rough cost |
|---|---|---:|
| Utility cart / push cart | carry system | $30–$100 |
| PVC / metal tube | nozzle and fan support | $10–$40 |
| Clamps / brackets | mount parts | $5–$25 |

## 11) Cheapest buying strategy

The cheapest good path is usually:

### Buy one basic 12V spot sprayer
That often already includes:
- tank
- pump
- hose
- some wiring

Then add:
- better nozzle
- main filter
- pressure gauge
- blower fan
- simple mounting parts

### Budget ideas

| Build type | Approx. cost |
|---|---:|
| smallest first test | $80–$150 |
| useful one-sided test build | $150–$220 |
| better two-sided greenhouse build | $200–$350 |

## 12) The exact order to connect the liquid side

Use this order:

```text
Tank
 ↓
Fill screen
 ↓
Pump
 ↓
Main line filter
 ↓
Pressure gauge
 ↓
Ball valve
 ↓
Tee / manifold
 ├──> tip filter -> nozzle
 └──> tip filter -> nozzle
```

If you later use 4 nozzles, the tee becomes a bigger manifold.

### Why this order matters

- the pump gets relatively clean liquid
- the main filter protects the downstream system
- the gauge shows working pressure
- tip filters catch the last small particles before the nozzle

---

## 13) The exact order to build the fan side

### One-sided version

```text
blower -> air stream -> nozzle spray enters air -> crop
```

### Two-sided version

```text
left blower + left nozzle group -> left crop
right blower + right nozzle group -> right crop
```

### Best fan mounting ideas

- fan behind nozzle
- fan slightly above nozzle
- fan beside nozzle, pointed across the mist path

### What matters most

The droplets must be pulled or pushed into moving air **immediately**.

---

## 14) Good geometry to start with

You asked for real implementation details, so here is a simple starting geometry.

### Starting geometry

- nozzle to crop edge: **20–40 cm**
- fan to nozzle: **very close**
- nozzle angle: **slightly inward**
- fan angle: **along aisle into crop**
- nozzle heights:
  - lower nozzle: about 30–50 cm high
  - upper nozzle: about 70–100 cm high
- fan speed: enough to move leaves gently

### What “good” should look like

- outer leaves get coverage
- inner leaves get some coverage too
- little liquid drips from leaves
- much less liquid reaches the ground
- the air stream does not blast the crop too hard

---

## 15) How to prevent clogging after long use

This is one of your biggest concerns, and it is a real problem.

### Why clogging happens

- dirty water
- undissolved product
- solids in pesticide
- hard water scale
- dried residue
- poor cleaning
- too-small nozzle opening

### Best anti-clog system

Use **three filter levels**.

#### Level 1 — Fill screen
At the tank opening.

Stops:
- dust
- plastic pieces
- rust
- dirt
- leaf pieces

#### Level 2 — Main line filter
After the pump.

A **50-mesh** filter is a good practical starting point.

#### Level 3 — Tip filter
Before each nozzle.

Usually:
- 50 mesh or
- 100 mesh

depending on the nozzle and liquid.

### Best cleaning routine

Every time after spraying:

1. empty or handle leftover chemical correctly
2. rinse the tank
3. fill with clean water
4. run clean water through all hoses and nozzles
5. remove nozzle tips
6. remove tip strainers
7. wash them
8. brush gently if needed
9. inspect for damage
10. store clean

### Important rule

Do **not** clean nozzles with:
- pin
- steel wire
- needle
- nail

That damages the orifice.

Use:
- soft brush
- water
- proper cleaning solution if needed

### Long-use maintenance habit

Keep spare:
- nozzles
- tip filters
- seals
- hose clamps

Because field maintenance is much easier with spares.

---

## 16) How to know the spray is too coarse or too fine

### If spray is too coarse

You will see:
- big droplets
- leaf dripping
- puddles on the floor
- poor inner canopy reach

Fixes:
- slightly more pressure
- better hollow-cone nozzle
- a bit more fan help
- reduce flow if needed
- move sprayer closer

### If spray is too fine

You will see:
- cloud hangs in the air
- mist drifts away
- hard to see wetting on leaves
- more exposure risk

Fixes:
- slightly lower pressure
- slightly larger nozzle
- less fan speed
- shorter spray distance
- more focused direction

---

## 17) How to tune the nozzle and fan together

This is the real “secret” of the build.

### Tuning steps

1. run with water only
2. start with low fan speed
3. start with moderate spray pressure
4. watch droplet behavior
5. increase fan slowly
6. watch leaf movement
7. check floor wetness
8. check inner canopy coverage
9. adjust nozzle angle
10. repeat

### Best result

You want:
- fine droplets
- leaves move gently
- good inside coverage
- low runoff
- no huge floating cloud

### Bad result

If the leaves shake strongly:
- fan is probably too strong

If the floor gets wet fast:
- droplets are probably too large or flow is too high

If a cloud hangs in the greenhouse:
- droplets are probably too fine or airflow is wrong

---

## 18) How to test it correctly

### Step 1 — Water only
Never start with insecticide.

### Step 2 — Put cards or paper in these places

- top of canopy
- outer leaf area
- inner canopy
- lower leaf area
- underside if possible
- floor

### Step 3 — Compare
Check:
- which areas get droplets
- how much reaches the floor
- whether airflow improves inside coverage

### Simple success rule

A good setup should give:
- more coverage on plant cards
- less liquid on ground cards

---

## 19) Real problems you may face during production or repeated use

### Problem 1 — nozzle blocks often
Fix:
- better filtering
- better cleaning
- better mixing
- ceramic nozzles
- keep spares

### Problem 2 — pump pressure pulses
Fix:
- add regulator or pulsation damper if needed
- shorten unstable hose layouts
- use a more stable pump if budget allows

### Problem 3 — spray pattern changes over time
Fix:
- nozzle wear check
- replace worn tips
- clean strainers
- inspect pressure

### Problem 4 — fan pushes too hard
Fix:
- lower fan speed
- use PWM
- change blower angle
- move slightly farther from crop

### Problem 5 — fan too weak
Fix:
- stronger blower
- two blowers
- better nozzle/fan alignment
- move closer to the crop

### Problem 6 — chemical settles in tank
Fix:
- use gentle return line / recirculation if the chemical label and mixture allow it

### Problem 7 — seals and hoses wear out
Fix:
- use sprayer-rated chemical-resistant materials
- inspect regularly
- rinse every time

### Problem 8 — electrical issues in humid greenhouse
Fix:
- fuse near power source
- protect connectors
- keep wiring away from spray
- use waterproof switch if possible

### Problem 9 — poor lower-leaf coverage
Fix:
- add lower nozzle
- angle lower nozzle upward a little
- reduce speed of movement

### Problem 10 — too much chemical reaches operator
Fix:
- no one in spray path
- proper PPE
- good greenhouse safety routine
- follow product label

## 20) Best first prototype I would personally build

If I had to choose one low-cost version for you, it would be this:

### Hydraulic system
- 10–15 gallon tank
- 12V diaphragm pump, 40–70 PSI
- fill screen
- 50-mesh main filter
- 0–60 PSI gauge
- tee manifold
- 2 tip filters
- 2 ceramic hollow-cone nozzles on left
- 2 ceramic hollow-cone nozzles on right (optional second stage)

### Air system
- 1 blower for left side
- 1 blower for right side
- each close to its nozzle group
- optional PWM control

### Frame
- push cart in aisle
- vertical left and right supports
- adjustable nozzle and blower brackets

### Operating style
- move down the aisle slowly
- spray short controlled passes
- keep nozzles 20–40 cm from crop edge
- tune fan so leaves move gently

### Why this design is good
Because it is:
- affordable
- simple
- serviceable
- expandable
- not over-complicated

---

## 21) Things I would NOT buy first

Because your budget is limited, avoid buying these first:

- expensive electrostatic kits
- thermal foggers
- advanced greenhouse precision sprayers
- AI cameras
- robotic carts
- expensive rotary atomizers
- ultra-micro fog systems

First prove:
> fan + nozzle + correct droplet range works in your greenhouse

Then upgrade later if needed.

---

## 22) Best implementation plan

### Phase 1
Build a one-sided test rig.

Buy:
- one pump/sprayer base
- one hollow-cone nozzle
- one blower
- one filter
- one gauge

Goal:
- verify the concept

### Phase 2
Build a two-sided aisle system.

Add:
- second blower
- second nozzle group
- cart
- better mounts

Goal:
- real row spraying

### Phase 3
Improve reliability.

Add:
- spare parts kit
- cleaning routine
- fan speed control
- maybe two-level nozzles
- maybe return line

Goal:
- long-term use

---

## 23) Best answer in plain words

If you want the simplest direct answer:

- Use **fine mist**, not room-filling fog
- Aim around **50–100 microns**
- Start around **70–100 microns**
- Use a **ceramic hollow-cone nozzle**
- Use a **12V blower fan close to the nozzle**
- Use a **50-mesh main filter** and **tip filters**
- Flush the whole system after every use
- Use **water only** for the first tests
- For a real greenhouse setup, use **two sides of the aisle**
- If possible, use **two nozzle heights per side**

That is the best practical low-cost way to make your idea real.
